name: Liquid facelift
lead: 'Liquid facelift' is a marketing term for non-surgical facial rejuvenation that uses injectable fillers, often hyaluronic acid, to restore volume and contour in several areas of the face in one session. [1][2][3] The term is also used in one 2018 case series for a different technique: water jet-assisted liposuction used alongside surgical rhytidectomy. [4]

Injectable fillers are classified by the US FDA as medical devices. Wikipedia reports that most wrinkle fillers are temporary, lasting about six months, and lists bruising, lumps, infection and, rarely, vision loss from vascular embolization among risks. [5]

paras: A 2010 article in Missouri Medicine describes a blending of surgical and nonsurgical techniques driven by patients' desire for an un-operated look and shorter recovery, and discusses volume loss in the facial skeleton and soft-tissue compartments, contrasting autologous fat grafting and injectable fillers with surgical rhytidectomy. [2] A 2009 nurse-practitioner article and a 2024 oral and maxillofacial surgery atlas chapter are titled 'The liquid facelift' and 'Liquid Facelift'. [3][6]

A 2018 case series of 25 patients (median age 56) in the Journal of Plastic, Reconstructive & Aesthetic Surgery reported first experience using facial water jet-assisted liposuction for facial contouring, fat harvesting and hydrodissection of the skin flap in surgical facelifts, under the heading 'liquid facelift'. [4] No randomized controlled trial of the filler-based liquid facelift was identified in the sources consulted.

Wikipedia reports that common filler effects include bruising, redness, pain and itching, less commonly infection and allergic reactions causing lumps or scarring, and rarely permanent vision loss or delayed skin necrosis from embolization. In the US only a small number of fillers are approved; in the UK and EU a CE mark certifies production standards without requiring proof of efficacy. Who may inject fillers is debated between physicians and other licensed injectors. [5]

card.summary: Marketing term for filler-based non-surgical facial rejuvenation; the literature is mostly reviews, with no controlled trials found.
card.note: Rare filler complications include vascular embolization and vision loss.

quick.overview:
A liquid facelift uses injectable fillers, usually hyaluronic acid, in several facial areas to restore volume and contour without surgery. The phrase is a marketing term and is also used for one surgical water-jet technique.

The sources found are narrative reviews and a 25-patient surgical case series, not controlled trials.
quick.mechanism: Fillers are placed to replace volume lost with aging in facial compartments. Most wrinkle fillers are temporary, lasting about six months according to Wikipedia.
quick.risks: Common effects are bruising, redness and pain. Rare but serious risks include infection, lumps, vascular embolization and permanent vision loss. Fillers are FDA-regulated medical devices.
